meaning.evidence: Every beat is kept in order: the house-party contrast, "Liberty Hall", eight and eight-twenty, the creak, the pictures, the books and inscription, Emerson, "Only ten past nine!", dressing quietly. The 1902 photo is now "in a dinner suit" and "in his uni music club", fair equivalents.

sense.evidence: Terms fit: "What time's brekkie?", "nothing you can really hang your hat on" for nothing to take hold of, "Pretty scruffy-looking bunch", "dodgy-looking barges", "Oh, righto then!", "almost on the sly".

authenticity.evidence: Natural Australian speech ("Let's have a squiz at the pictures", "Fair enough, I s'pose."), though the opener "Okay, so take getting up in the morning" sounds more generic modern than Australian.

register.evidence: A light touch at level 2, clean: "brekkie", "squiz", "uni", "dodgy", "righto", with the rest in plain modern English.

tone.evidence: The gentle comic self-mockery survives: "Never touch a sonnet before breakfast.", "Reckon they thought that'd be over your head, did they? Well, we'll show them!"

flow.evidence: Reads easily aloud: "So it's back over on the cool pillow till eight-twenty. Then up on your elbow again, head cocked to one side."

variety.evidence: Varied, though "brekkie" is used twice: "What time's brekkie?" and "heading down to brekkie!"

essence.evidence: Clearly the same sketch, but some of the period wit is flattened: "It's fine at the time, but come the morning it's so vague it's downright scary.", "Forget the bath, too noisy."

problems.quote: Okay, so take getting up in the morning, for example.
problems.original: Take, for example, the matter of arising in the morning.
problems.why: Added "Okay, so" is generic chat filler and jars with the period setting.

problems.quote: it's so vague it's downright scary
problems.original: there is a vagueness about it that is simply terrifying
problems.why: Loses the mock-grand phrasing that carries the humour.

A.summary: A natural, accurate light-touch retelling; slightly modernised and flatter than the original's mock-grand voice.

meaning.evidence: Every point kept, closely: "there's likely to be a frightful mix-up", "Maybe eleven o'clock is their Sunday getting-up time.", "Only ten past nine!"

sense.evidence: Terms fit: "The feeling behind it is perfectly bonzer" matches "bully" (excellent), "Pretty scruffy-looking mob", "dodgy-looking barges", "Oh, righto!", "So they reckoned".

authenticity.evidence: Natural on the whole; "perfectly bonzer" is dated, but the period setting carries it. "mob" and "go out for a wander round the grounds" sound right.

register.evidence: Light level-2 touch, clean: "bonzer", "mob", "dodgy", "righto", "reckoned", "on the sly".

tone.evidence: Keeps the mock-dramatic comedy: "come morning there's a vagueness about it that's downright terrifying", "It's the work of a moment to leap out of bed", "Deathly silence".

flow.evidence: Smooth throughout; only "Scratch the bath as too noisy." is slightly stiff.

variety.evidence: No term repeated; slang spread thinly and evenly: "bonzer", "mob", "dodgy", "righto", "reckoned", "wander".

essence.evidence: Unmistakably the original: keeps its rhythm and its mock-grand phrasing, "Any more sleep is out of the question.", "We'll read it just out of spite."

problems.quote: Scratch the bath as too noisy.
problems.original: Eliminate the tub as too noisy.
problems.why: "Scratch ... as" is a slightly stiff join.

B.summary: Faithful and light, keeping the original's comic voice with well-placed Aussie touches; the strongest of the three.

meaning.evidence: Mostly the original verbatim, but the quoted inscription is altered: "To my beaut friends the Elbridges", which puts slang into a quoted 1907 dedication.

sense.evidence: "Too right, where there is a large house-party" uses an agreement reply in place of the connective "Of course"; "To my beaut friends" is wrong in a quoted dedication; "At what time is brekkie?" clashes with its formal frame.

authenticity.evidence: Slang dropped into untouched 1920s prose: "At what time is brekkie?", "Let's take a squiz"; "perfectly bully" and "if you started your tub" left as is.

register.evidence: Largely untranslated, lighter than level 2: "Let us say that you awake at eight." and nearly every sentence as written.

tone.evidence: The original's tone carries through, but "Too right" at the start jars against the stately mock-formality.

flow.evidence: Original prose reads well, but the swaps produce clunky joins: "Too right, where there is a large house-party the problem is a simple one", "At what time is brekkie?"

essence.evidence: It is the original text, so its shape and character are whole: "Eliminate the tub as too noisy. And so, very cautiously, almost clandestinely, you proceed to dress."

problems.quote: Too right, where there is a large house-party
problems.original: Of course, where there is a large house-party
problems.why: "Too right" is an emphatic agreement reply, not a connective; wrong sense.

problems.quote: To my beaut friends the Elbridges
problems.original: To my good friends the Elbridges
problems.why: Alters a quoted inscription written by someone else; wrong sense and voice.
Slang dropped into a formal sentence.

problems.quote: Let us say that you awake at eight.
problems.original: Let us say that you awake at eight.
problems.why: Representative: left largely untranslated against the brief.

C.summary: The original with a few misplaced word swaps, two of them wrong-sense; too light and jarring where it does change.
